title: Freedom and Necessity
question: Can freedom coexist with a world explained through causes?
sources: Kant, Critique of Pure Reason; Schopenhauer, The World as Will and Representation; Nietzsche, Beyond Good and Evil

chapters.name: The central problem
chapters.body: Welcome to the Grand Academy. Today we are examining: Can freedom coexist with a world explained through causes? The figures guiding this discussion are Kant · Schopenhauer · Nietzsche. Kant distinguishes a phenomenal order governed by causal laws from the standpoint of practical reason. The difficulty is not solved by declaring human decisions exempt from nature. The critical question is how a person can be regarded as responsible without treating freedom as an observable event among other events.

chapters.name: The argument
chapters.body: Schopenhauer radicalizes the challenge. Individual actions can be intelligible through motives while the character manifesting them is not simply chosen at will. His distinction between empirical willing and the deeper Will disrupts the everyday identification of freedom with choosing between alternatives.

chapters.name: A philosophical counterpoint
chapters.body: Nietzsche interrogates the moral psychology concealed in claims about free will, especially the wish to assign praise, guilt and punishment. His polemic is not identical to Schopenhauer’s metaphysics, and neither thinker simply repeats Kant’s account of autonomy.

chapters.name: The difficulty
chapters.body: Test the meaning of the word free in each position. Does it signify exemption from causes, self-legislation, transparency to one’s motives, or the possibility of assuming responsibility? A solution that shifts between these senses has not yet answered the problem.

chapters.name: Your reflection
chapters.body: As this seminar concludes, consider the following. Describe an action you regard as free. Identify what a causal explanation could show about it without necessarily settling its moral significance. Return to the central question: Can freedom coexist with a world explained through causes? Record which premises you would accept, which demand further justification, and what would count as a good objection.

title: The Dialectic of Recognition
question: Does self-consciousness require another self-consciousness?
sources: Hegel, Phenomenology of Spirit; Fichte, Foundations of Natural Right; Sartre, Being and Nothingness

chapters.name: The central problem
chapters.body: Welcome to the Grand Academy. Today we are examining: Does self-consciousness require another self-consciousness? The figures guiding this discussion are Hegel · Fichte · Sartre. In Hegel’s Phenomenology, the encounter with another self-consciousness destabilizes any claim to self-sufficient independence. Recognition cannot be adequately understood as a private psychological feeling. It concerns an intersubjective structure in which one consciousness seeks acknowledgement from another.

chapters.name: The argument
chapters.body: The lordship-and-bondage episode explores the instability of asymmetrical recognition. The dominant figure seeks confirmation from someone treated as dependent, raising the question whether such recognition can possess the authority originally sought.

chapters.name: A philosophical counterpoint
chapters.body: Fichte’s account of a summons to freedom and Sartre’s description of being seen by another illuminate different dimensions of the problem. One foregrounds reciprocal practical relations; the other can expose conflict, objectification and shame.

chapters.name: The difficulty
chapters.body: Do not reduce this dialectic to a simple social parable or assume that all three thinkers share an identical theory of personhood. Ask which kinds of mutual dependence actually follow from each argument.

chapters.name: Your reflection
chapters.body: As this seminar concludes, consider the following. Can respect be secured by force? Explain why domination might undermine the very recognition it demands. Return to the central question: Does self-consciousness require another self-consciousness? Record which premises you would accept, which demand further justification, and what would count as a good objection.

title: Being and the Question of Meaning
question: Why distinguish Being from the entities that are?
sources: Heidegger, Being and Time; Aristotle, Metaphysics; Husserl, Ideas I

chapters.name: The central problem
chapters.body: Welcome to the Grand Academy. Today we are examining: Why distinguish Being from the entities that are? The figures guiding this discussion are Heidegger · Aristotle · Husserl. Heidegger begins from the claim that understanding entities presupposes an often-unexamined familiarity with what it means for something to be. The ontological difference is not a division between two objects: Being is not an additional entity waiting alongside the rest.

chapters.name: The argument
chapters.body: The analysis of Dasein approaches the question through a being for whom its own existence is an issue. The everyday world is initially disclosed through involvement and use, not necessarily through detached theoretical observation.

chapters.name: A philosophical counterpoint
chapters.body: Aristotle’s investigations of being qua being and Husserl’s phenomenological attention to intentional givenness offer important contexts, yet Heidegger’s question cannot be converted without remainder into classical ontology or a theory of inner consciousness.

chapters.name: The difficulty
chapters.body: If Being is not another thing, how does philosophical language speak meaningfully about it? A convincing interpretation must avoid the temptation to reify the very condition under investigation.

chapters.name: Your reflection
chapters.body: As this seminar concludes, consider the following. Choose a familiar tool. Explain how its significance differs when you use it from when you inspect it as a detached object. Return to the central question: Why distinguish Being from the entities that are? Record which premises you would accept, which demand further justification, and what would count as a good objection.

title: The Problem of Knowledge
question: What distinguishes knowledge from a compelling belief?
sources: Plato, Theaetetus; Descartes, Meditations; Hume, Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding

chapters.name: The central problem
chapters.body: Welcome to the Grand Academy. Today we are examining: What distinguishes knowledge from a compelling belief? The figures guiding this discussion are Plato · Descartes · Hume. Plato’s dialogues examine why true belief may fail to offer a stable account of what is known. Rational justification appears necessary, yet the difficulty lies in specifying which kind of account actually transforms belief into knowledge.

chapters.name: The argument
chapters.body: Descartes introduces methodical doubt to test whether a secure foundation can survive skeptical challenges. His search for certainty must be distinguished from the claim that all ordinary experience is useless or always false.

chapters.name: A philosophical counterpoint
chapters.body: Hume turns attention toward habits of inference, especially the transition from observed conjunctions to claims about necessary connections. The skeptical problem is sharpened because successful prediction alone need not demonstrate rational necessity.

chapters.name: The difficulty
chapters.body: Do not confuse infallibility, justification and empirical reliability. These are different candidate standards, and each encounters its own counterexamples. An account that protects certainty by denying almost all ordinary knowledge may be too restrictive.

chapters.name: Your reflection
chapters.body: As this seminar concludes, consider the following. What evidence would you need to say you know that tomorrow will resemble yesterday? Return to the central question: What distinguishes knowledge from a compelling belief? Record which premises you would accept, which demand further justification, and what would count as a good objection.

title: What Is a Good Life?
question: Is flourishing a feeling, a practice, or a kind of character?
sources: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics; Epicurus, Letter to Menoeceus; Marcus Aurelius, Meditations

chapters.name: The central problem
chapters.body: Welcome to the Grand Academy. Today we are examining: Is flourishing a feeling, a practice, or a kind of character? The figures guiding this discussion are Aristotle · Epicurus · Stoics. Aristotle characterizes flourishing through excellent activity rather than a passing sensation. The practical difficulty concerns the cultivation of stable dispositions and the role of luck, community and external goods.

chapters.name: The argument
chapters.body: Epicurean reflection seeks freedom from disturbance but is frequently misunderstood as an invitation to unlimited pleasure. Its conception of prudent desire often emphasizes moderation and friendship.

chapters.name: A philosophical counterpoint
chapters.body: Stoic ethics foregrounds the discipline of judgment and the distinction between what is within our agency and what is not. That focus does not imply that vulnerability or political responsibility simply disappear.

chapters.name: The difficulty
chapters.body: The traditions disagree about the standing of external conditions. If poverty or illness can seriously obstruct flourishing, is virtue alone sufficient? If virtue is sufficient, what makes another person’s suffering morally urgent?

chapters.name: Your reflection
chapters.body: As this seminar concludes, consider the following. Describe a flourishing life and decide whether your criteria concern feelings, achievements, relationships or exercised virtues. Return to the central question: Is flourishing a feeling, a practice, or a kind of character? Record which premises you would accept, which demand further justification, and what would count as a good objection.

title: The Will and Its Suffering
question: Does human desire necessarily involve suffering?
sources: Schopenhauer, The World as Will and Representation; Dhammapada; Nietzsche, The Gay Science

chapters.name: The central problem
chapters.body: Welcome to the Grand Academy. Today we are examining: Does human desire necessarily involve suffering? The figures guiding this discussion are Schopenhauer · Buddhism · Nietzsche. Schopenhauer reads individual striving against a deeper metaphysical background: satisfaction is unstable because the restless Will continually renews desire. He develops this thesis using experience, embodiment and a distinctive reading of Kant.

chapters.name: The argument
chapters.body: Buddhist discussions of craving and dependent arising often make suffering intelligible without positing a single metaphysical Will underlying all appearances. Similarity in the diagnosis of craving must not erase fundamental differences in ontology.

chapters.name: A philosophical counterpoint
chapters.body: Nietzsche contests life-denying evaluations and asks whether struggle can be affirmed rather than simply extinguished. This response cannot be reduced to the optimistic claim that suffering is always beneficial.

chapters.name: The difficulty
chapters.body: Ask whether the experience of wanting is sufficient to prove a universal metaphysical principle. Separate the description of dissatisfaction, the diagnosis of its cause and the proposed mode of release.

chapters.name: Your reflection
chapters.body: As this seminar concludes, consider the following. Can a project be intrinsically meaningful if completing it never removes the possibility of wanting again? Return to the central question: Does human desire necessarily involve suffering? Record which premises you would accept, which demand further justification, and what would count as a good objection.

title: Language and the Limits of Thought
question: Can philosophical confusion arise from how we use words?
sources: Frege, On Sense and Reference; Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations; Heidegger, On the Way to Language

chapters.name: The central problem
chapters.body: Welcome to the Grand Academy. Today we are examining: Can philosophical confusion arise from how we use words? The figures guiding this discussion are Wittgenstein · Frege · Heidegger. Frege’s logical investigations distinguish sense and reference, enabling philosophical questions about how expressions contribute to thought. Logical clarification can expose hidden structural differences beneath familiar grammar.

chapters.name: The argument
chapters.body: The earlier Wittgenstein explores the relation between meaningful propositions and the logical representation of facts. His later work shifts attention to practices, forms of life and the plurality of language-games.

chapters.name: A philosophical counterpoint
chapters.body: Heidegger emphasizes the historical and disclosive character of language in ways not reducible to semantic analysis. These approaches should not be fused into the easy slogan that language creates everything.

chapters.name: The difficulty
chapters.body: A useful test asks whether a dispute persists after the use of its key terms has been clarified. But there are philosophical disagreements that are not exhausted by linguistic therapy, even when language plays a crucial part.

chapters.name: Your reflection
chapters.body: As this seminar concludes, consider the following. Find a philosophical question that changes when you distinguish two senses of the same word. Return to the central question: Can philosophical confusion arise from how we use words? Record which premises you would accept, which demand further justification, and what would count as a good objection.

title: Morality and Its Foundations
question: Can moral demands be grounded in duty, consequences, or character?
sources: Kant, Groundwork; Mill, Utilitarianism; Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics

chapters.name: The central problem
chapters.body: Welcome to the Grand Academy. Today we are examining: Can moral demands be grounded in duty, consequences, or character? The figures guiding this discussion are Kant · Mill · Aristotle. Kant’s ethics evaluates the maxim of action in relation to principles that can claim universal validity. The central question concerns rational consistency and respect, not merely obedience to whatever social rule happens to exist.

chapters.name: The argument
chapters.body: Mill’s utilitarianism judges conduct by its relation to happiness and suffering. Its sophistication depends upon how consequences are understood and whose interests enter the calculation.

chapters.name: A philosophical counterpoint
chapters.body: Aristotelian ethics investigates the cultivation of practical wisdom and the formation of character within a human life. Virtuous judgment is not simply another algorithm for maximizing a numerical score.

chapters.name: The difficulty
chapters.body: Consider a truthful statement that predictably causes harm. Consequences, rules and cultivated judgment may recommend different considerations. A fair comparison must specify each tradition’s strongest response.

chapters.name: Your reflection
chapters.body: As this seminar concludes, consider the following. Can a good intention justify a disastrous result, or should consequences always decide the issue? Return to the central question: Can moral demands be grounded in duty, consequences, or character? Record which premises you would accept, which demand further justification, and what would count as a good objection.

title: Science, Explanation, and Positivism
question: What entitles a method to call itself scientific?
sources: Comte, Course of Positive Philosophy; Hume, Enquiry; Popper, Logic of Scientific Discovery

chapters.name: The central problem
chapters.body: Welcome to the Grand Academy. Today we are examining: What entitles a method to call itself scientific? The figures guiding this discussion are Comte · Hume · Popper. Comte’s positivism proposes that mature inquiry attends to regularities accessible to disciplined investigation rather than explanations invoking inaccessible essences. His hierarchy of the sciences carries both methodological and social ambitions.

chapters.name: The argument
chapters.body: Hume’s treatment of induction places pressure on any easy identification of repeated observation with a logically necessary law. The challenge survives successful scientific practice.

chapters.name: A philosophical counterpoint
chapters.body: Popper later emphasizes testability and the critical exposure of conjectures to possible refutation. His position must not be collapsed into either Comte’s historical scheme or the later verificationist doctrines of logical positivism.

chapters.name: The difficulty
chapters.body: Ask whether scientific explanation merely describes regularities or also investigates mechanisms and causal structures. A restrictive account of science risks excluding legitimate inquiry by definition.

chapters.name: Your reflection
chapters.body: As this seminar concludes, consider the following. Propose an apparently scientific claim and explain what observation would genuinely count against it. Return to the central question: What entitles a method to call itself scientific? Record which premises you would accept, which demand further justification, and what would count as a good objection.

title: The Subject and the World
question: Is experience primarily subjective, relational, or embodied?
sources: Husserl, Ideas I; Heidegger, Being and Time; Merleau-Ponty, Phenomenology of Perception

chapters.name: The central problem
chapters.body: Welcome to the Grand Academy. Today we are examining: Is experience primarily subjective, relational, or embodied? The figures guiding this discussion are Husserl · Heidegger · Merleau-Ponty. Husserl’s phenomenological reduction redirects attention to the structures through which objects are given to consciousness. Intentionality does not mean that consciousness is a sealed container filled with private images.

chapters.name: The argument
chapters.body: Heidegger begins from being-in-the-world, challenging accounts that derive worldly involvement from a detached subject encountering independently posited objects. His analysis foregrounds practical familiarity.

chapters.name: A philosophical counterpoint
chapters.body: Merleau-Ponty makes embodiment central to perception. The lived body is neither merely a physiological object nor an immaterial observer occupying such an object.

chapters.name: The difficulty
chapters.body: These projects share a descriptive concern without having identical starting points. The distinction between a condition of disclosure and a psychological cause of perception must be carefully preserved.

chapters.name: Your reflection
chapters.body: As this seminar concludes, consider the following. When you reach for a book, what is given before you formulate an explicit judgment about it? Return to the central question: Is experience primarily subjective, relational, or embodied? Record which premises you would accept, which demand further justification, and what would count as a good objection.

title: Justice and the Ideal City
question: Can a just society be defined independently of its citizens?
sources: Plato, Republic; Aristotle, Politics; Rawls, A Theory of Justice

chapters.name: The central problem
chapters.body: Welcome to the Grand Academy. Today we are examining: Can a just society be defined independently of its citizens? The figures guiding this discussion are Plato · Aristotle · Rawls. Plato’s Republic investigates justice through an analogy between the ordering of a soul and the arrangement of a city. The analogy is philosophically contentious rather than a straightforward proof of a political blueprint.

chapters.name: The argument
chapters.body: Aristotle approaches political association through practices of citizenship and inquiry into constitutions. His account exposes how purposes and institutional forms matter to practical judgment.

chapters.name: A philosophical counterpoint
chapters.body: Rawls constructs a device of representation in which principles are selected without privileged knowledge of one’s eventual position. This should not be mistaken for a historical description of an actual contract.

chapters.name: The difficulty
chapters.body: Ask whether justice is chiefly a property of persons, institutions or relationships. A political order may appear orderly while distributing recognition or opportunity unequally.

chapters.name: Your reflection
chapters.body: As this seminar concludes, consider the following. Could a well-ordered city be unjust to one of its members? Defend your standard. Return to the central question: Can a just society be defined independently of its citizens? Record which premises you would accept, which demand further justification, and what would count as a good objection.

title: The Self and Its Continuity
question: What, if anything, persists through personal change?
sources: Dhammapada; Hume, Treatise of Human Nature; Locke, Essay Concerning Human Understanding

chapters.name: The central problem
chapters.body: Welcome to the Grand Academy. Today we are examining: What, if anything, persists through personal change? The figures guiding this discussion are Buddhism · Hume · Locke. Buddhist analyses of non-self investigate the conditions under which experiences arise, challenging the assumption that experience requires an independent and unchanging owner.

chapters.name: The argument
chapters.body: Hume’s introspective investigations do not discover a simple enduring impression of the self. The problem becomes how identity is attributed across succession and association.

chapters.name: A philosophical counterpoint
chapters.body: Locke connects personal identity with consciousness and memory, raising familiar puzzles concerning forgotten events, duplication and the scope of responsibility.

chapters.name: The difficulty
chapters.body: Do not infer from the denial of a permanent substance that ordinary agency or ethical responsibility must be impossible. Each view must explain what continuity can mean without presupposing what is at issue.

chapters.name: Your reflection
chapters.body: As this seminar concludes, consider the following. Imagine a person who forgets a formative event. What exactly, if anything, has ceased to persist? Return to the central question: What, if anything, persists through personal change? Record which premises you would accept, which demand further justification, and what would count as a good objection.

title: Truth, Genealogy, and Suspicion
question: What can an account of the origins of a belief establish?
sources: Nietzsche, Beyond Good and Evil; Marx, German Ideology; Freud, Introductory Lectures

chapters.name: The central problem
chapters.body: Welcome to the Grand Academy. Today we are examining: What can an account of the origins of a belief establish? The figures guiding this discussion are Nietzsche · Marx · Freud. Nietzsche’s genealogical inquiry interrogates the historical and psychological conditions through which evaluations acquire apparent self-evidence. A genealogy does not automatically refute a claim merely by finding its origins.

chapters.name: The argument
chapters.body: Marx’s critique of ideology directs attention to social relations and material interests that influence the production of thought. These claims require substantive historical and economic argument.

chapters.name: A philosophical counterpoint
chapters.body: Freud’s interpretation of psychic conflict introduces motives that may not be transparent to conscious reflection. This is not a license to diagnose any disagreement as repression.

chapters.name: The difficulty
chapters.body: The genetic fallacy remains a danger for traditions of suspicion: explaining why a proposition was adopted does not, without further premises, establish whether it is true or false.

chapters.name: Your reflection
chapters.body: As this seminar concludes, consider the following. Can a morally admirable conviction have an unflattering origin without losing its validity? Return to the central question: What can an account of the origins of a belief establish? Record which premises you would accept, which demand further justification, and what would count as a good objection.

title: The Infinite and the Absolute
question: Can finite differences belong to an intelligible whole?
sources: Spinoza, Ethics; Hegel, Science of Logic; Schelling, Philosophical Investigations into Freedom

chapters.name: The central problem
chapters.body: Welcome to the Grand Academy. Today we are examining: Can finite differences belong to an intelligible whole? The figures guiding this discussion are Spinoza · Hegel · Schelling. Spinoza’s substance metaphysics treats finite modes as intelligible through a reality not reducible to their independent existence. His account demands care with notions of necessity and freedom.

chapters.name: The argument
chapters.body: Hegel’s discussion of infinity and determination rejects a picture in which the infinite is merely another object beyond the finite. The logical question concerns relations that generate and transform determination.

chapters.name: A philosophical counterpoint
chapters.body: Schelling’s philosophical development introduces distinctive accounts of identity, nature and freedom, resisting easy assimilation to any single system of the Absolute.

chapters.name: The difficulty
chapters.body: The temptation is to turn the Absolute into an oversized finite entity. A stronger reconstruction asks what explanatory work the concept does and whether the totality can be articulated without suppressing difference.

chapters.name: Your reflection
chapters.body: As this seminar concludes, consider the following. Can a whole explain its parts without rendering their individual histories philosophically irrelevant? Return to the central question: Can finite differences belong to an intelligible whole? Record which premises you would accept, which demand further justification, and what would count as a good objection.

title: Religion and the Limits of Reason
question: Does faith answer questions reason cannot settle?
sources: Aquinas, Summa Theologiae; Kant, Religion within the Bounds of Bare Reason; Kierkegaard, Fear and Trembling

chapters.name: The central problem
chapters.body: Welcome to the Grand Academy. Today we are examining: Does faith answer questions reason cannot settle? The figures guiding this discussion are Aquinas · Kant · Kierkegaard. Aquinas distinguishes philosophical demonstration from truths known through revelation. His account of reason and faith should not be caricatured as the claim that every article of belief has a proof.

chapters.name: The argument
chapters.body: Kant restricts the scope of theoretical claims regarding objects beyond possible experience while reconfiguring questions of religion within practical reason.

chapters.name: A philosophical counterpoint
chapters.body: Kierkegaard’s pseudonymous investigations challenge the assumption that existential commitment can be captured by detached objective system-building. His literary forms complicate attempts to ascribe every sentence directly to the author.

chapters.name: The difficulty
chapters.body: If evidence cannot establish a religious commitment, does this make the commitment irrational, supra-rational, or simply of another kind? Distinguish the positions before evaluating them.

chapters.name: Your reflection
chapters.body: As this seminar concludes, consider the following. What would count as a misuse of reason in matters of faith, and who decides? Return to the central question: Does faith answer questions reason cannot settle? Record which premises you would accept, which demand further justification, and what would count as a good objection.

title: Mind and Machine
question: Could an artificial system genuinely understand?
sources: Descartes, Meditations; Turing, Computing Machinery and Intelligence; Searle, Minds, Brains, and Programs

chapters.name: The central problem
chapters.body: Welcome to the Grand Academy. Today we are examining: Could an artificial system genuinely understand? The figures guiding this discussion are Descartes · Turing · Searle. Descartes distinguishes thinking substance from extended substance in a system that makes consciousness central to knowledge of the self. The mind-body problem cannot simply be read backward into every modern discussion of computation.

chapters.name: The argument
chapters.body: Turing proposes an operational discussion of machine intelligence through performances in conversation, shifting away from an inaccessible inspection of inner essences.

chapters.name: A philosophical counterpoint
chapters.body: Searle’s Chinese-room argument contests the sufficiency of formal symbol manipulation for understanding. Critics dispute the scope of its conclusion and whether an entire system could possess what an individual component lacks.

chapters.name: The difficulty
chapters.body: Differentiate intelligence, consciousness, understanding and linguistic competence. An experiment establishing one may not establish the others. Nor does uncertainty about consciousness imply that all performance is meaningless.

chapters.name: Your reflection
chapters.body: As this seminar concludes, consider the following. Would a perfectly convincing philosophical interlocutor necessarily understand its own answers? Return to the central question: Could an artificial system genuinely understand? Record which premises you would accept, which demand further justification, and what would count as a good objection.

title: The Meaning of History
question: Can history be intelligible without being predetermined?
sources: Vico, New Science; Hegel, Lectures on the Philosophy of History; Marx, German Ideology

chapters.name: The central problem
chapters.body: Welcome to the Grand Academy. Today we are examining: Can history be intelligible without being predetermined? The figures guiding this discussion are Vico · Hegel · Marx. Vico treats historical understanding as an inquiry into institutions, language and human making. Historical knowledge differs from abstract speculation because practices develop through collective life.

chapters.name: The argument
chapters.body: Hegel’s philosophy of history asks how freedom may become intelligible through historically determinate forms. The claim requires careful interpretation and does not license simplistic assertions that every event was justified.

chapters.name: A philosophical counterpoint
chapters.body: Marx foregrounds forms of production, class relations and material conditions, though the complexity of historical change resists reduction to a one-variable mechanical law.

chapters.name: The difficulty
chapters.body: Distinguish explanation after the fact from prediction before the fact. An account that gives meaning to historical transformations need not possess a reliable formula for future events.

chapters.name: Your reflection
chapters.body: As this seminar concludes, consider the following. Can an event be historically significant without having been necessary? Return to the central question: Can history be intelligible without being predetermined? Record which premises you would accept, which demand further justification, and what would count as a good objection.

title: Beauty and Disinterested Judgment
question: Why does beauty matter if it serves no immediate purpose?
sources: Kant, Critique of Judgment; Schopenhauer, World as Will and Representation; Nietzsche, Birth of Tragedy

chapters.name: The central problem
chapters.body: Welcome to the Grand Academy. Today we are examining: Why does beauty matter if it serves no immediate purpose? The figures guiding this discussion are Kant · Schopenhauer · Nietzsche. Kant investigates judgments of taste as reflective evaluations that solicit agreement without applying a determinate concept. Disinterestedness is not indifference to whether beauty exists.

chapters.name: The argument
chapters.body: Schopenhauer describes aesthetic contemplation as a temporary suspension of ordinary willing, interpreting art in relation to a metaphysics of suffering and release.

chapters.name: A philosophical counterpoint
chapters.body: Nietzsche develops distinctive accounts of the artistic and affirmative possibilities of life. His later writings cannot simply be mapped onto Schopenhauer’s negative assessment of willing.

chapters.name: The difficulty
chapters.body: Ask whether an artwork is valuable because of the pleasure it affords, the truth it discloses, or its capacity to alter how the viewer lives. These criteria may coincide, but they need not.

chapters.name: Your reflection
chapters.body: As this seminar concludes, consider the following. Can an unsettling artwork be beautiful without being pleasurable? Return to the central question: Why does beauty matter if it serves no immediate purpose? Record which premises you would accept, which demand further justification, and what would count as a good objection.

title: Time and Lived Experience
question: Is time a sequence of moments or a structure of experience?
sources: Augustine, Confessions XI; Bergson, Time and Free Will; Husserl, Lectures on Time-Consciousness

chapters.name: The central problem
chapters.body: Welcome to the Grand Academy. Today we are examining: Is time a sequence of moments or a structure of experience? The figures guiding this discussion are Augustine · Bergson · Husserl. Augustine’s reflections on time reveal the difficulty of identifying past and future as available objects in precisely the way present things appear to be. Memory and expectation transform the problem.

chapters.name: The argument
chapters.body: Bergson contrasts lived duration with spatialized measures that divide change into countable units. The distinction is not a rejection of clocks but an inquiry into their explanatory limits.

chapters.name: A philosophical counterpoint
chapters.body: Husserl’s lectures on internal time-consciousness examine retention, primal impression and protention as a structure through which a temporal object can be experienced as enduring.

chapters.name: The difficulty
chapters.body: Do not mistake a phenomenology of time for a physical theory of measurement. A plausible account of consciousness must still explain succession without imagining a second internal clock.

chapters.name: Your reflection
chapters.body: As this seminar concludes, consider the following. When listening to a melody, why is the note you just heard still relevant to the note sounding now? Return to the central question: Is time a sequence of moments or a structure of experience? Record which premises you would accept, which demand further justification, and what would count as a good objection.

title: Nature, Ecology, and Responsibility
question: Does nature have value independently of human interests?
sources: Aristotle, Physics; Spinoza, Ethics; selected contemporary environmental ethics

chapters.name: The central problem
chapters.body: Welcome to the Grand Academy. Today we are examining: Does nature have value independently of human interests? The figures guiding this discussion are Aristotle · Spinoza · Contemporary ethics. Aristotle’s teleological investigations approach living beings through characteristic activities and ends. A contemporary ethics of ecosystems cannot be inferred directly from this biological framework.

chapters.name: The argument
chapters.body: Spinoza understands humans as belonging to an intelligible natural order rather than standing outside it. The account of conatus complicates stark oppositions between self-preservation and natural necessity.

chapters.name: A philosophical counterpoint
chapters.body: Modern environmental ethics asks whether moral considerability extends beyond persons, perhaps to sentient creatures, species, habitats or ecological wholes. Different proposals carry different kinds of obligations.

chapters.name: The difficulty
chapters.body: A claim that everything in nature is valuable risks lacking guidance when values conflict. An adequate environmental ethic must confront tragic choices, uncertainty and unequal human vulnerability.

chapters.name: Your reflection
chapters.body: As this seminar concludes, consider the following. If preserving a forest harms an economically dependent community, how should competing responsibilities be assessed? Return to the central question: Does nature have value independently of human interests? Record which premises you would accept, which demand further justification, and what would count as a good objection.

title: Introducing Pre-Socratic Philosophy
question: What is at stake in From myth to inquiry?
sources: Course thematic guide: Pre-Socratic Philosophy — From myth to inquiry; consult a verified edition before attributing a passage.

chapters.name: Why this tradition matters
chapters.body: Welcome to the Grand Academy course capsule on Pre-Socratic Philosophy. Our opening problem is From myth to inquiry. From myth to inquiry in Pre-Socratic Philosophy brings six concepts into one explanatory problem. Begin by distinguishing Physis, the natural order investigated through reasoned explanation, from Archê, a first principle proposed to account for nature's diversity. Their difference is important precisely because substituting one for the other changes the question being asked. Next consider Mythos: traditional narrative explanations of cosmic origin. Ask how this third term qualifies the first distinction, rather than assuming that the three are

chapters.name: Conceptual distinctions
chapters.body: Begin with two distinctions. Physis: the natural order investigated through reasoned explanation Archê: a first principle proposed to account for nature's diversity Ask what each idea explains and where the two must not be confused.

chapters.name: Competing interpretation
chapters.body: In the chapter’s interpretive setting, Logos refers to a rational account capable of being argued about. Compare this with Cosmos, understood here as the ordered world considered as an intelligible whole. The relation could be one of support, dependence, tension, or merely historical association. The correct relation must be argued rather than guessed from proximity. Formulate a test case that would require Logos but not

chapters.body: One may object that Physis does not entail Archê. What supporting premise would be Reconsider the central distinction in Pre-Socratic Philosophy: which premise would have to be changed to answer this objection?

title: Introducing Socratic Philosophy
question: What is at stake in Socrates and the polis?
